background.definition: Roseola (also called exanthem subitum or roseola infantum) is an acute febrile illness characterized by three to four days of fever followed by the development of a maculopapular rash. It presents most commonly in the first two years of life. Risk factors include age, day care attendance, older siblings in the home, and female sex.

list.listitem: Virtually all children in the United States have antibodies by 2 years of age (20% by 12 months and 77% by 24 months).
The peak age of infection is between 9 and 21 months.
Worldwide there is geographic variation in the incidence of roseola.
Roseola is caused by human herpesviruses (HHV) 6 and 7.
Most children are infected by HHV-6 type B.
Roseola is spread by respiratory droplets of asymptomatic individuals.
The child is most infectious during the viremic phase.
The double-stranded DNA virus activates a specific lymphoproliferative response. Natural killer cells appear to be activated acutely, with specific lymphocytic activity developing later on.
HHV-6 type B is thought to be more prevalent than type A.

Differential.Differential_Features: Does not have clear three- to four-day history of fever preceding rash
Has additional symptoms of coryza, Koplik spots
Often difficult to differentiate if patient has not yet defervesced and characteristic rash has not appeared; often leads to unnecessary workups before diagnosis can be made
Typically exanthems occur prior to fever or with the onset of fever (not after defervescence)
Rash enlarging with characteristic target lesions with central clearing and confluent; usually no fever present
Petechial rash occurring with the fever; child toxic looking
Purpuric rash often confined to buttocks and lower extremities; no preceding fever
Petechial rash beginning on palms and soles
Sandpapery rash, more confluent; child often presenting additional symptoms of sore throat and abdominal pain
Child toxic appearing; peeling rash, desquamating
Five or more days of fever, often also presenting >1.5 cm anterior cervical lymph nodes, mucous membrane changes, extremity changes (swollen hands, feet), nonpurulent conjunctivitis
Pustular rash becoming scabbed over, pruritic; fever with rash
Red tender nodules over pretibial surfaces
Fever before onset of rash; pyruia

list.listitem: Typically roseola presents in the child less than 3 years of age with a three- to four-day prodrome of fever to 40 degrees Celsius.
Rash begins to appear when fever abates.
Discrete, pink, morbilliform rash that often starts centrally (chest/trunk) and spreads to extremities. Often the scalp is involved. Rash may involve the entire body.
Other symptoms include mild diarrhea (68%), erythematous papules in the pharynx (65%), cough (50%), mild cervical lymph node swelling (31%), and eyelid swelling (30%).
A small case-control study with 46 patients found that uvulo-palatoglossal junction ulcers had a 90% positive predictive value when present and 100% negative predictive value when absent.
Complications include febrile seizure (6%-15%), encephalitis (<1%), possibly intussusception, and meningitis (<1%).
Diagnostic testing is not routinely recommended but may be needed in cases of meningitis or encephalitis or if the presentation is not typical.

Although routine studies are not recommended, if laboratory values are obtained, the definitive test is isolation of the virus from peripheral blood lymphocytes, saliva, and CSF during the febrile phase of the infection.
Detection of IgM antibodies is not reliable, but seroconversion from negative to positive is good evidence for infection.
A rapid method to detect herpesvirus 6 in serum using loop-mediated isothermal amplification demonstrated high sensitivity (95.5%) and specificity (95.2%).

Diagnosis is made by characteristic history and physical findings. Roseola is an acute febrile childhood illness with characteristic three- to four-day prodrome of high fever followed by defervescence and the appearance of a discrete, pink, morbilliform rash that often starts centrally (chest/trunk) and spreads to extremities. Often the scalp is involved.
The child usually is alert and nontoxic.
The rash usually begins to fade within three to four days.
Over half of the patients have uvulopalatoglossal ulcers.
Complications include seizures, meningitis, and encephalitis, although these are rare.
Diagnostic testing is not routinely recommended, but seroconversion from negative to positive is strong evidence for infection.
Children with roseola may present with sterile pyuria.
Good supportive care with adequate hydration is important. C
Antipyretics (acetaminophen) may be used for fever during the initial febrile phase of the illness. C
Antipyretics (acetaminophen ) may be used for fever during the initial febrile phase of the illness.
There is some evidence that ganciclovir may help treat HHV-6 in immunocompromised patients.
Treatment is supportive. Fever may be treated with acetaminophen or ibuprofen (if the child is older than 6 months of age). Aspirin should not be used.
Attention to hydration is important. Parents should be encouraged to offer frequent small amounts of fluids.
Hospitalize for meningitis/encephalitis or inability to tolerate fluids.
Treat with antiepileptics if the child has more than a simple febrile seizure, as with encephalitis.
Provide IV fluid support if the child cannot tolerate or is unable to take in oral fluids.
Serious complications are rare and occur more often in immunocompromised individuals.
See Management of complications.
This is a self-limited illness, and 96% of patients completely recover within 10 days. The median range for recovery is 9 days, with a range of 4 to 15 days. B
